title: An ensemble figure asks one question: what is common to repeat runs, and how large is the run-to-run spread around it?
summary: Eight repeat flame runs are aligned at ignition and then compared by frame, by time series, by distribution, by spectrum and by onset time. Reading any of these figures means separating what repeats from run to run (the central curve) from what does not (the spread), and asking which kind of spread each band draws.

media.alt: Time series of flame height in millimetres against time in seconds after ignition, from minus 10 to about 530 s. A black median line rises from about 5 mm at ignition to about 33 mm at 90 s inside a tan band labelled combined uncertainty plus or minus ten; after about 150 s the grey 95 percent envelope and darker interquartile band become a dense noisy cloud between about 50 and 175 mm.

source.caption: Ensemble flame height, ignition-aligned
source.note: Eight repeat n-heptane pool-flame runs, each aligned to its own ignition time. This page teaches how to read ensemble figures: frame matrices, an aligned time series with bands, a violin plot, a spectrum, a phase average, an onset-time bar chart and a forest-style robustness check. The same eight runs (MVI_8032, 8033, 8036, 8037, 8040, 8041, 8042, 8049) appear throughout.

read_the_figure.question: Across eight repeats of the same experiment, how does flame height develop after ignition, and how much of the scatter is run-to-run variation versus measurement uncertainty?
read_the_figure.axes: Ensemble time series: x is time in seconds after each run's own ignition (about -10 to 530 s), y is flame height in millimetres (about 0 to 200). Frame matrices: one row per run, one column per time after ignition, every cell the same field of view. Violin and onset charts: one category per run. Spectrum: x is frequency in Hz (0 to 12), y is log10 of power.
look_at: Time series: the black line is the cross-run median. The darker band is the interquartile range (IQR, the middle half of the runs). The light band is the 95 percent envelope over n = 8 runs. The tan band is a separate thing: the combined measurement uncertainty, drawn only where the figure shows it (the first 90 s or so).

Frame matrices: read across a row to see one run develop, down a column to compare runs at the same time after ignition. Differences in brightness and size at the same column are run-to-run differences.

Violin plot: the width of each shape is how often that height occurred; the middle tick is the median and the end caps are the minimum and maximum. One run (MVI_8042) sits near 33 mm while the others sit near 110 to 140 mm.
Spectrum: the black line is the mean of log-power across runs and the grey band is the 95 percent envelope. A repeating oscillation would show as a bump above the line.
Onset chart: one bar per run, a dashed line at the mean. MVI_8042 has no bar, so the mean is over seven runs.
Phase cycle: the x axis is the fraction of one puff cycle, not time. A real cycle would make the median curve rise and fall once across the axis.
read_the_figure.proves: If the median is smooth and the combined-uncertainty band is narrower than the run-to-run band, then the trend is a property of the experiment and not of one lucky run. If the bands overlap everywhere, the runs cannot be distinguished at the stated uncertainty.
if_wrong: A median that looks smooth only because few runs contribute at that time: after about 90 s the aligned traces in the figure do not all cover the same time range, so the median there rests on fewer runs than eight.
A band that is called an envelope but is really the extremes of a few runs: with n = 8 a '95 percent envelope' is close to min and max, so it widens with every outlier.
A flat or featureless spectrum: no coherent oscillation, or one hidden near the highest frequency drawn (see Nyquist below).
A run that is out of family (MVI_8042) pulling the ensemble: check whether it should be in the ensemble at all before reading the mean.
must_check: The band is named and its meaning stated (IQR, envelope, standard error, expanded uncertainty). Here the tan band's unit is cut off in the legend: it reads 'combined uncertainty plus or minus 10'.
The number of runs contributing at each time is shown or stated. It is not shown here beyond n = 8 in the legend.
Time is aligned to a defined event (ignition) and the same event definition is used for every run.
Units agree between figures: the phase-cycle figure labels its y axis in px, while its median value (about 120) looks like millimetres in the other figures.
Every run in the study is either shown or its omission is explained: MVI_8042 is absent from the long frame matrix and from the onset chart.
as_drawn: All values are read off by eye and are approximate (about 5 to 10 percent).
Ensemble height (03): the median rises from about 5 mm at 0 s to about 33 mm at 90 s. Between roughly 200 and 530 s the cloud of traces sits mostly between 75 and 150 mm, centred near 110 to 120 mm.
Run medians from the violin plot (05): about 128, 119, 110, 110, 118, 131, 33 and 141 mm for runs 8032, 8033, 8036, 8037, 8040, 8041, 8042 and 8049. Seven of the eight lie between 110 and 141 mm.
Onset time (31): about 160, 200, 193, 197, 173, 203 and 167 s for seven runs, with the figure's own mean of 184.6 s. The sample standard deviation of those seven read-off values is about 18 s.
Anchored-only check (32): three run means of about 127, 108 and 116 mm and an ensemble mean of about 117 mm with a wide bar from about 108 to 124 mm.
Spectrum (30): mean log10 power falls from about 4.7 at the lowest frequency to about 2 near 6 to 8 Hz and then rises to about 3 near 12 Hz. No isolated peak is visible at this scale.
Phase cycle (04): the median is flat at about 120 on the axis, and the grey envelope spans from about 40 to about 1020.

terms.meaning: A set of repeat runs of the same experiment. Statistics across the ensemble describe what is reproducible.
Time measured from each run's own ignition instant, so that runs started at different moments can be overlaid.
The middle value across runs and the range holding the middle half of them. Both are robust to a single outlier run.
The range holding 95 percent of the runs at each time. With only eight runs it is close to the minimum and maximum.
The uncertainty of one measurement after adding the independent sources (pixel scale, edge position and so on) in quadrature, following the GUM.
How the variance of a signal is spread over frequency. A coherent oscillation shows as a peak.
Half the frame rate. Frequencies above it cannot be told apart from lower ones in sampled data.
Cut the record into cycles, label each sample by its fraction of a cycle, and average samples with the same label. It recovers the shape of a repeating cycle from noisy data.
A mirrored density estimate of a distribution, with the median and range marked.

remember: A centre line without a named band is not a result. Always ask what each shaded region is the spread of.
Run-to-run spread and measurement uncertainty are different things and need different bands.
With n = 8 runs, an empirical 95 percent envelope is nearly the full range.
Repeatability is read from the bars, not the mean: a mean of 184.6 s says little until you see how far each run sits from it.
A spectrum can only show frequencies up to half the frame rate.

understand.title: Why align at ignition
understand.text: Runs are started by hand, so wall-clock time is arbitrary. Subtracting each run's own ignition time puts the physically meaningful event at zero, so that the same column of the frame matrix means the same stage of development for every run.

understand.title: Three different spreads
understand.text: The IQR and the 95 percent envelope describe how much the runs differ from one another. The tan uncertainty band describes how well one measurement of one flame is known. A narrow tan band inside a wide grey band says the scatter is real flame behaviour; the reverse says it is mostly measurement noise.

understand.title: Why a violin and an onset bar chart are drawn as well
understand.text: A time series hides which runs are unusual. The violin shows each run's whole height distribution and exposes the run (MVI_8042) that stayed small. The onset chart shows each run's one scalar against the mean so that repeatability is visible rather than summarised.

understand.title: Why a robustness check
understand.text: The anchored-only figure repeats the estimate on a subset chosen for a cleaner width definition. If the conclusion does not move when the data are restricted, it does not depend on that choice. With only three runs in the subset, the interval is wide, which is itself the honest result.

steps.title: Align the runs
steps.note: Each run i is shifted by its own ignition time so that tau = 0 is the same physical event in every run.

steps.title: Median across runs at each aligned time
steps.note: The median ignores a single outlier run. It is defined only at times where several runs have data.

steps.title: Empirical interval across runs
steps.note: An order-statistics interval. With eight runs the 95 percent envelope drawn in practice is the extreme order statistics or close to them, which is why it behaves like a min-max band.

steps.title: Measurement uncertainty adds in quadrature
steps.note: Independent sources combine as the root of the sum of squares (GUM). This is the quantity the tan band is built from; it describes one measurement, not the spread between runs.

steps.title: Mean and standard error across runs
steps.note: For the onset times the mean is the dashed line. The standard error says how well the mean of the campaign is known, which is smaller than the spread of single runs by the factor square root of n.

steps.title: A small sample needs a t interval
steps.note: With seven onset times the multiplier is about 2.45, not 1.96. Using the normal value would make the interval too narrow.

steps.title: Sampling limits the spectrum
steps.tex: f_N=\frac{f_s}{2},\qquad f_{\mathrm{alias}}=\left|\,f-m f_s\,\right|\ \text{for the integer } m \text{ giving } f_{\mathrm{alias}}\le f_N
steps.note: A video at 24 frames per second can represent frequencies only up to 12 Hz, which is where the spectrum axis ends. A frequency above 12 Hz folds back and appears below it.

steps.title: Phase averaging
steps.note: If the cycle is real and its period is known, the average of many cycles shows the cycle shape with the noise averaged down. If the period is wrong, the average is flat. A flat phase average therefore means no cycle at the assumed period, not a small cycle.

worked.title: Mean, spread and a t interval for the onset times
worked.problem: Reading the onset chart (31) by eye gives about 160, 200, 193, 197, 173, 203 and 167 s for seven runs. Compute the mean, the standard deviation and a 95 percent t interval for the mean.

solution.text: Sum the values and divide by seven.
The sample standard deviation, from the squared deviations with n minus one.
The standard error, and the t multiplier for six degrees of freedom (2.447).

worked.answer: Mean about 185 s (the figure's own mean is 184.6 s), run-to-run standard deviation about 18 s, and a 95 percent interval for the campaign mean of about 185 plus or minus 16 s. Single runs spread far more than the mean is uncertain.

analyze.q: The median in the headline figure is drawn with a tan uncertainty band only up to about 90 s. What would you need to be told to trust the median at 300 s, and what does the dense cloud there tell you about the number of contributing runs?
analyze.hint: Think about whether all eight runs have data at the same aligned time, and what an order-statistics band does with few runs.

analyze.q: The violin plot shows one run near 33 mm and seven near 110 to 140 mm. Three explanations are possible: that run never developed, it was measured differently, or it is a real part of the variability. How would you separate them using the frame matrices in this group?
analyze.hint: Compare the 0 to 90 s matrix with the 0 to 240 s matrix and note which runs appear in each.

analyze.q: In the spectrum the mean log power rises again towards 12 Hz. List two standard explanations and say which extra information you would need.
analyze.hint: Frame rate, aliasing of faster motion, and the noise floor of the edge detector.

evaluate.q: Is it legitimate to call the grey band a '95 percent envelope' when n = 8? What would you call it, and which band would you draw instead for the uncertainty of the mean?
evaluate.hint: Order statistics and the standard error.

evaluate.q: The phase-averaged figure is presented as recovering the puff cycle, but its median curve is flat. Does this show that there is no cycle? List what else it could show.
evaluate.hint: Wrong period, a period drifting between runs, averaging over different cycles, or a cycle too fast for the frame rate.

create: Redraw the headline figure so that the number of runs contributing at each time is a thin strip under the axis, and the tan band is labelled with its unit and its confidence level.
Design an onset-time figure for the campaign that shows every run as a point with its own uncertainty bar, the mean with a t interval, and a marked place for runs that never reached flickering.
Plan a replacement for the phase-cycle figure that first estimates the dominant period run by run, then phase-averages each run separately and overlays the eight curves.

checks.q: Why are the runs aligned at ignition rather than plotted against clock time?
checks.hint: What differs between runs besides the flame?
checks.answer: Because the start of each recording is arbitrary. Aligning on each run's own ignition puts the same physical event at zero, so that the same time after ignition means the same stage of development.

checks.q: Three run means are 127, 108 and 116 mm. What is their mean and standard error?
checks.hint: Sample standard deviation with n minus one, divided by the square root of three.
checks.answer: The mean is 117 mm. The sample standard deviation is about 9.7 mm, so the standard error is about 5.6 mm.

checks.q: The tan band is narrow compared with the grey band. What does that say about the scatter in the data?
checks.hint: Which band describes one measurement and which describes the spread across runs?
checks.answer: That most of the scatter is real variation between runs or in time, not measurement error. The tan band is the uncertainty of one measurement; the grey band is how far the runs differ.

checks.q: A spectrum of flame height from 24 frames per second video shows no peak up to 12 Hz. Does that prove the flame has no oscillation?
checks.hint: What can a sampled record not represent, and what does averaging over runs do to a peak whose frequency moves?
checks.answer: No. Frequencies above 12 Hz are not represented and would fold back, and a peak whose frequency differs from run to run is smeared by averaging log power across runs. The figure shows only that no common peak is visible at this scale.

checks.q: How would you make a phase-averaged cycle trustworthy?
checks.hint: Estimate the period first, and check the result on each run separately.
checks.answer: Estimate the dominant period from each run's own spectrum, cut that run into cycles of its own period, phase-average within the run, and then overlay the per-run curves with their spread. State the period used and the number of cycles averaged.
